content:
"* The article is introducing writer Jeffrey Eugenides and the serious ideas in one of his stories. It says that even back in 2005, he believed that the more people learn about their country, the more reasons they may find to feel ashamed. The interviewer points out that many painful events happened after that, like Hurricane Katrina, the money crisis, and major political changes. So the question is whether shame about America now feels even bigger than shame about personal mistakes. Eugenides answers that both kinds of shame are deeply connected. He means that a country is made of ordinary people, so national problems also live inside personal lives. In simple terms, he is saying that the bad parts of American history and the bad parts of our own past can both weigh on us at the same time. That idea creates a strong tension between private feelings and public events. The article uses this as a highlight of his thoughtful and sad view of modern America.

* The article also describes where he is being interviewed and why that setting matters. He is speaking at Princeton, where he has taught for years, in a new library that is still unfinished. A paper sign marked “unisex” on a restroom door is used to show how much attitudes about gender have changed. The writer says that years ago, Eugenides often had to explain the meaning of “intersex” when talking about his famous novel Middlesex. Now those topics are more familiar in public life, so the setting helps welcome readers into that social change. This part suggests that culture has moved, even if many problems remain. It also reminds us that Eugenides is known for writing about identity, history, and the body. You could say the passage connects politics, gender, and personal life in one scene. There is no mention of a girlfriend directly, but the emotional style is intimate enough to feel close to everyday relationships. In a broad sense, it also touches on social and emotional health, because shame, identity, and belonging affect how people live."
